reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Retronychia is proximal ingrowing of the nail, in which the plate is driven backwards into the proximal nail fold rather than into the lateral folds
It typically affects the great toenail and presents with proximal pain, swelling, redness, and chronic inflammation of the proximal fold
Recurrent granulation tissue and discharge from beneath the proximal fold are characteristic, and it is often misdiagnosed as simple chronic paronychia
A key sign is the arrest of normal distal nail growth, with newer nail plates stacking up behind the leading plate
It usually follows trauma or repetitive microtrauma that disrupts the normal attachment and forward growth of the plate
Onychoscopy and imaging such as ultrasound can support the diagnosis by demonstrating the embedded proximal plate and stacked nails
The definitive treatment is avulsion of the affected nail plate, which relieves the inflammation and allows a new, correctly aligned nail to grow
reference.pathophysiology: Retronychia arises when the longitudinal growth of the nail plate is interrupted, usually after trauma, so that the plate loses its normal forward advance and is instead pushed proximally into the tissue of the proximal nail fold. Continued matrix activity produces new plates behind the disconnected leading nail, and these become stacked one beneath another, embedding into the proximal fold. The buried plate acts as a foreign body, provoking persistent inflammation, granulation tissue, and discharge, which explains why the condition mimics and is frequently confused with chronic paronychia.
additionalDifferentials: Pyogenic granuloma of the nail fold
Nail changes of psoriasis affecting the proximal fold
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment for proximal fold inflammation with arrested distal nail growth
Onychoscopy to detect stacked nail plates and proximal embedding
Ultrasound to demonstrate multiple overlapping plates when the diagnosis is unclear
Swab of any discharge if secondary bacterial infection is suspected
History of preceding trauma or repetitive microtrauma
Review for coexisting nail disease or predisposing footwear factors
redFlags: Persistent proximal fold inflammation unresponsive to treatment for presumed paronychia
Signs of spreading soft-tissue infection requiring prompt intervention
Atypical granulation or a mass suggesting an underlying tumour
Recurrent disease after treatment indicating incomplete removal or ongoing trauma
reference.prognosis: Retronychia responds well to nail plate avulsion, after which inflammation settles and a normally growing nail usually returns, although recovery takes months and recurrence can occur if predisposing trauma continues.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating retronychia as chronic paronychia with antimicrobials or topical agents alone
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of arrested distal nail growth
Delaying avulsion, which prolongs the inflammation unnecessarily
Failing to address ongoing trauma or footwear factors, leading to recurrence
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
